parts.name: Daymet weather, basin means (CAMELS basin_mean_forcing/daymet)
parts.kind: weather interpolated from weather-station readings to a 1 km grid, averaged over the basin
parts.what_it_is: Daymet is a daily 1 km gridded weather data set for North America, derived solely from daily station observations of temperature and precipitation: stations are interpolated with an iterative method and a truncated Gaussian filter, and the Mountain Climate Simulator (MT-CLIM) estimates shortwave radiation and humidity (Newman et al. 2015, Sect. 2.2). CAMELS gives the area-weighted mean over each basin outline, computed by the USGS Geo Data Portal. Columns as shipped: dayl (s), prcp (mm/day), srad (W/m2), swe (mm), tmax (C), tmin (C), vp (Pa); the models read prcp, srad, tmax, tmin, vp, dayl (swe, snow-water equivalent, is not used).
parts.producer: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (Daymet; Thornton et al.); basin means by NCAR and the USGS Center for Integrated Data Analytics for CAMELS
parts.version: unverified: not stated in the CAMELS readme files, nor in Newman et al. 2015 or Addor et al. 2017, which cite 'Daymet: Daily surface weather on a 1 km grid for North America, 1980-2012' (Thornton et al. 2012, ORNL DAAC); the project could only date it to before Daymet version 4 (2021)
parts.spatial_grid: 1 km grid (Newman et al. 2015), averaged to one value per basin with area weights; the 12 basins are 113 to 1,928 km2
parts.time_stamp: the rain of 'day d' ends at about 09:00 local standard time on day d (median basin 08:48; basins 07:26 to 18:16; four readings 07:28 to 10:42; measured against hourly rain in results/day_windows.json). So the afternoon and evening rain of the issue day is filed under the next day. Consistent with the rain-gauge observers' day: Daymet version 4 (2021) documents the effect and corrects it, and CAMELS (2015, extended 2016) predates that version (published readings: published_reading_of_the_day); the other Daymet variables were not measured.
parts.latency_real_time: none: a finished research data set (1980-2014)

published_reading_of_the_day.reference: Thornton, P. E., Shrestha, R., Thornton, M., Kao, S.-C., Wei, Y., Wilson, B. E. (2021). Gridded daily weather data for North America with comprehensive uncertainty quantification. Scientific Data, 8, 190.
what_it_says: It is the paper of Daymet version 4.
Daily precipitation observations that are taken once a day but not from midnight to midnight local standard time can put all or part of a rain event on the wrong calendar day.
In version 4 the recorded precipitation of stations with a time of observation before noon local standard time is shifted back one day.
This timing bias was not examined in earlier versions of Daymet.
published_reading_of_the_day.not_said: It does not mention CAMELS. That CAMELS holds an earlier version follows from the dates only: CAMELS was published in 2015, Daymet version 4 in 2021.

published_reading_of_the_day.reference: Kratzert, F., Klotz, D., Hochreiter, S., Nearing, G. S. (2021). A note on leveraging synergy in multiple meteorological data sets with deep learning for rainfall-runoff modeling. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, 25, 2685-2703.
what_it_says: A lag-correlation analysis of the precipitation products in CAMELS found a higher correlation between Daymet and Maurer when Maurer was lagged by one day in 325 of 531 basins.
Gridded products differ in how they define a calendar day.
published_reading_of_the_day.not_said: It does not say at what hour the Daymet day ends.

datasets.name: NOAA AORC v1.1 (Analysis of Record for Calibration)
datasets.kind: an hourly rain analysis anchored on rain gauges and radar, made after the fact
datasets.what_it_is: The gridded record of near-surface weather of NOAA's National Weather Service Office of Water Prediction; the project reads its hourly total precipitation (APCP_surface). It is an analysis, not an observation: a daily rain total is fixed first and then spread over the 24 hours. Daily total: NLDAS-2 gauge-based 24-hour totals ending 12 UTC for 1979-2001, NCEP Stage IV radar-and-gauge totals with manual quality control from 2002; both bias-corrected with monthly Livneh totals (1979-2015 where available). Hours: the hourly shape of Stage IV where radar and satellite exist, GDAS where they do not, other sources before the radar era (the reading of the NWS methods document in results/review_aorc_rain_to_midnight.json). So the hours of the training years 1980-2000 are daily totals spread by non-radar sources; the hours of the test years follow the radar.
datasets.producer: NOAA National Weather Service, Office of Water Prediction (OWP); copy on AWS Open Data
datasets.version: AORC version 1.1 (version 1.0 was completed in November 2019; 1.1 addresses its issues: AWS registry). AWS announced on 2026-04-02 that about 0.04% of the rows were masked by error and that the Zarr files are being regenerated: data/aorc is kept as the reference copy (sha256 of the 12 basin files in results/aorc_data.json, amendments)
datasets.spatial_grid: 30 arc-second latitude-longitude grid (1/120 degree, about 0.8 km, called 1 km here; 4,201 x 8,401 cells); a basin = the cells whose centre lies inside its outline: 159 to 2,649 cells
datasets.period_used: 1980-09-25 00:00:00 to 2014-10-05 23:00:00 UTC (hour-ending stamps): 298,296 hours at each of the 12 basins
datasets.time_stamp: hour-ending, UTC: the value stamped T is the rain of the hour that ends at T (methods document p.10; checked against Stage IV hourly files on test-year storm days: correlation 0.98 at lag 0, 0.73 and 0.72 at lags +1 and -1); the project sums it over the wall-clock day of each gauge
datasets.latency_real_time: about 10 days (AWS registry: 'The data creation runs with a 10-day lag to ensure the inclusion of any corrections to the input Stage IV and NLDAS data'): not a real-time product

datasets.turned_into_input: basin mean = the plain mean of the cells whose centre lies inside the outline (their areas differ by under 1% within a basin), one value per hour; 408 of 3,579,552 basin-hours (4 basins, runs of 48 to 120 hours) held no valid cell and were filled with the ERA5 hourly rain and flagged; 264 hours with some cells missing keep the mean of the others. Summed over the wall-clock day of the gauge (zoneinfo, summer time included): aorc_to_midnight (extra input of E1b, set wqa), aorc_to_09 (the window of the rain table, a control), aorc_utc_day (a control); in wqa_rep it replaces the Daymet rain column. The AORC rain of the local days t+1 to t+3 (p1..p3) is the perfect rain forecast, an upper bound, and the reference of the GEFS bias factors.

documentation_quotes.quote: The gridded AORC precipitation dataset contains one-hour accumulated surface-precipitation (APCP) ending at the 'top' of each hour, in liquid water-equivalent units (kg/m^2 to the nearest .01 kg/m^2)

For the duration of the period of record, NLDAS2 daily precipitation was used as the reference for all areas except as noted. From 1979 to 2001, NLDAS2 24-hour totals ending at 1200 UTC were the daily reference over the CONUS. Stage IV daily precipitation, with interactive, manual quality control and the introduction of radar data, has been used since 2002.

Examination of Stage IV daily precipitation showed that, in some areas, it was consistently biased low during the winter months from 2002 to approximately 2009 as a result of limitations in radar capability for precipitation-type discrimination prior to the implementation of dual-polarimetric technology. [...] improved the accuracy of precipitation estimates substantially, from 2010 to the near-present.

the AORC daily precipitation between 1979 and 2015 was bias corrected with monthly accumulated Livneh data, where available. [...] After 2015, the Stage IV daily product was directly used without a bias correction procedure. After daily AORC input forcing data was bias-corrected for the long-term climatology, the daily time series were then disaggregated using available hourly data

AORC daily precipitation during and after 2010 is based on Stage IV, where available, with a bias correction factor, varying by month, applied. The bias correction is set by the ratio of the 6-year accumulations for the Livneh data to the Stage IV data, during 2010-2015.

For the more recent years, Stage IV hourly data has been used to disaggregate the daily precipitation grids blended from several datasets. [...] GDAS hourly precipitation is used to disaggregate the 24-hour AORC values to 1-hour values in the case that remote-sensing information from radar or satellite is unavailable.

Temporal downscaling from daily to hourly precipitation amounts is based on a multiplicative-correction approach. The multiplicative correction approach disaggregates, temporally, daily rainfall amounts to hourly amounts using factors. These factors are calculated by aggregating hourly grids to 0:00, 1:00, 2:00 ...23:00 time steps and dividing these amounts with the coincident daily grids. The hourly grids were calculated from the mosaic of datasets that were applied: Stage IV, GDAS, Stage II, CFSR, CMORPH, WSI NOWrad, and MDR.
The data creation runs with a 10-day lag to ensure the inclusion of any corrections to the input Stage IV and NLDAS data.

documentation_quotes.where: AWS Open Data registry page (announcement of April 2, 2026)
documentation_quotes.quote: [...] some brittle components of the AORC data processing pipelines that, by our estimations, have resulted in 0.04% of all available rows being incorrectly masked. We've resolved the issue and we are currently regenerating the Zarr files to ensure a complete record.

datasets.reviewer_reading: Reading: from 2002 the daily reference is Stage IV (24 h ending 12 UTC to the best of my knowledge) with manual quality control; the daily total is then spread over the hours by the Stage IV hourly shape (GDAS where radar and satellite are missing, MDR/NOWrad/Stage II/CMORPH/CFSR before the radar era). An hour before local midnight therefore belongs to the same 12 UTC gauge day as the hours from midnight to 07:00 (08:00 in summer) of the next morning, and can be scaled by a daily total that contains rain after the issue time. The channel exists by construction; whether it matters is an empirical question (d2-d6). All training years (1980-2000) are in the period of NLDAS2 totals and non-radar hourly sources, all test years in the Stage IV period. The 10-day production lag confirms that AORC is not a real-time product.

stages.title: Raw downloads
stages.words: 11 data products were read from public services: CAMELS-US by hand on 2026-10-02, the rest by script on 2026-10-03, 2026-10-07, 2026-10-08. About 73 GB were read (69 GB of it as recorded transfers: AORC, GEFS, Stage IV); 5.9 GB are kept under data/. No payment and no account is recorded for any of them.
stages.note: bytes of the products with no recorded transfer are the sizes of the stored files

stages.title: Audit of the basins
stages.words: 671 CAMELS basins -> 78 candidates (HUC regions 03 and 06, snow under 10% of precipitation, aridity under 1, 100-2,500 km2) -> 63 complete (no missing flow day or weather value over 1980-10-01 to 2014-09-30; 15 rejected) -> 12 chosen by rule (4 per landscape, evenly spaced in basin area; no flow statistic and no model score enters).

stages.title: Caches on disk
stages.words: Every download is cached so that a script runs again offline: data/derived (the daily tables of the basins, parsed once), data/hourly (ERA5 and MERRA-2 hourly rain, USGS 15-minute flow), data/satellite (IMERG and MERRA-2 daily), data/aorc (hourly basin means), data/gefs (reforecast rain and basin means); sizes as `du` reports them.

stages.title: Daily inputs per basin
stages.words: flood.load_data() reads the CAMELS files into one table per basin: 6 weather columns (prcp, srad, tmax, tmin, vp, dayl) and the flow in mm/day, 12,418 days, no value missing (149,016 basin-days); 10 basin properties are repeated on every day. Each experiment adds its own daily columns (rain to midnight, the forecast rain of days t+1..t+3 ...), built by its script.

stages.title: The split
stages.words: By the day of the forecast target: training 1980-10-01 to 2000-09-30 (7,305 days), validation 2000-10-01 to 2005-09-30 (1,826), test 2005-10-01 to 2014-09-30 (3,287); together 12,418. Training fits the weights, the scalers and the high-flow levels; validation chooses settings and the stopping point; the test years are only scored.
outputs: no file: the dates are constants of code/flood.py (the satellite-era split is recorded in results/satellite_inputs.json)

stages.title: Scaling and the high-flow level
stages.words: Each input is put on one scale with the mean and standard deviation of the training years only: x_scaled = (x - mean_train) / sd_train (weather columns pooled over the training basins; the flow as log(1 + q); the properties over the training basins). The high-flow level of a basin is the 95th percentile of its daily flow in the training years (2.62 to 7.86 mm/day over the 12 basins): a day above it is a high-flow day.
outputs: results/models/*.pt (key sc: the scalers of each saved network)

stages.title: Training
stages.words: One sequence-to-sequence LSTM (64 memory cells, 21,443 weights with the river gauge, 17 inputs) reads a basin day by day and forecasts the flow of the next 3 days at every day. Each update uses 32 random sequences of 730 days (365 days read, 365 scored) from the training years; every 100 updates the mean validation NSE is checked and training stops after 6 checks without a gain (at most 2,000 updates); the best state is kept. Three random seeds per input set.

stages.title: Forecasts stored
stages.words: Every forecast is stored by its target day in results/preds/<model>_<inputs>.npz: 189 prediction sets (111 of them single trainings), so any score can be recomputed without training; 78 trained networks are saved (results/models) with their scalers, and a reloaded network reproduces its stored forecasts bit for bit. The results files record 167 trainings.

stages.title: Scores
stages.words: Test years only: median NSE over the 12 basins, the onsets warned (an onset is a high-flow day whose forecast was issued while the river was still at or below the high-flow level: 611 in the test years), the false warnings, and a verdict by criteria fixed in advance (GO: pod >= 0.70 and far <= 0.30; CAUTION: csi >= 0.40 but not GO; otherwise NOT YET; pod = share of high-flow days that were warned; far = share of warnings that were false; csi = hits / (hits + misses + false alarms)). Headline, LSTM with the river gauge, 1 day ahead: median NSE 0.59, 19% of onsets warned, 59% of warnings false: NOT YET.

stages.title: Documents

flow_mm_per_day.title: River flow in mm per day
flow_mm_per_day.words: The USGS gives flow in cubic feet per second. One cubic foot is 0.0283168 cubic metres and a day has 86,400 seconds, so cfs x 0.0283168 x 86,400 is the volume that passed the gauge in the day, in cubic metres; dividing by the basin area in square metres gives metres of water over the basin, and x 1000 gives millimetres. Rain and flow are then in the same unit.
flow_mm_per_day.area: area_m2 is line 3 of the basin's forcing file (the geospatial-fabric polygon), not the GAGES-II area of the attribute table; the two differ by -3.5% to +5.5% in the 12 basins (results/basin_gis.json: largest 3.8%, Hyco Creek, NC)
flow_mm_per_day.check: recomputed from the raw flow files for all 149,016 basin-days: the largest difference from the cache is 0

basin_mean_with_overlap_weights.title: A basin mean with overlap-area weights
basin_mean_with_overlap_weights.words: A grid cell lies wholly or partly inside a basin. IMERG (0.1 degree) and GEFS (0.25 degree) cells are large against the basins, so every cell that overlaps the outline counts in proportion to the area of the overlap. For AORC (1/120 degree) and Stage IV (4.76 km) the cells are small, so the basin mean is the plain mean of the cells whose centre lies inside the outline (their areas differ by under 1% within a basin).
basin_mean_with_overlap_weights.formula: x_basin = sum_i (w_i x_i) / sum_i w_i, with w_i = area of the overlap of cell i with the basin outline (geodesic area on the GRS80 ellipsoid for IMERG, equal-area projection EPSG:5070 for GEFS)

value_at_the_centroid.title: A value at the basin centroid
value_at_the_centroid.words: ERA5 (the 0.25 degree grid point nearest the centroid, which Open-Meteo returns) and MERRA-2 (the 0.5 x 0.625 degree cell that holds the centroid) stand for the whole basin by one grid point or cell; the ERA5 point lies 4 to 16 km from the centroid of basins of 113 to 1,928 km2.
value_at_the_centroid.formula: x_basin = x(grid point or cell nearest the centroid)

local_day_sum.title: Rain of a local wall-clock day from hourly rain
local_day_sum.words: A forecast is issued at local midnight at the end of day t, and hourly rain is stamped in UTC by the end of the hour. Every hour is given to the local calendar day in which it ends, by the gauge's wall clock (zoneinfo: America/New_York for 11 basins, America/Chicago for Leaf River; summer time included), and the hours of a day are summed. A day has 24 hours, or 23 or 25 where the clocks change (34 days of 23 hours and 34 days of 25 hours in the 34 years). No hour after the issue time is summed: proved for every hour by the wall clock, in UTC time, by a second route from the time-zone rules, and by replacing the later hours with made-up values (15_rain_to_midnight.py, 16_aorc_rain_to_midnight.py).
local_day_sum.formula: R_t = sum of the hourly rain r_h over the hours h whose end lies in (00:00, 24:00] of local day t

where_each_daily_value_ends.title: Where each daily value ends (measured, local standard time)
where_each_daily_value_ends.words: Each day's value was compared with hourly rain over 24-hour windows shifted hour by hour; the window that fits best gives the hour at which the product's 'day d' ends. Daymet rain ends at about 09:00 on day d (median basin 08:48; basins 07:26 to 18:16), NLDAS rain at about 17:30 (17:40), IMERG and the daily MERRA-2 at the UTC day (19:00; 18:00 in Leaf River, MS), the river flow at local midnight; the Maurer day has no single end. The forecast is issued at local midnight, so the afternoon and evening rain of the issue day is filed under the next day in the Daymet table. The hourly references carry timing errors of their own of one to two hours (results/day_windows.json, calibration).

values.river_flow: local midnight (wall clock, summer time included)

scaled_inputs.title: Scaled inputs
scaled_inputs.words: Each column is put on one scale with the mean and standard deviation of the training years (1980-10-01 to 2000-09-30), pooled over the training basins; the flow enters as log(1 + q_mm); the 10 basin properties are scaled over the training basins. The values are fitted on the training years only, so nothing of the validation or test years leaks into the scale (recomputed here and equal to the scalers stored in a saved network).

nse.title: Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE)
nse.words: 1 minus the squared error of the forecast divided by the squared error of always forecasting the mean of the scored days: 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than that mean, below 0 is worse. Scored per basin and lead on the test years; the median over the basins is reported.

worked.model: LSTM with the river gauge, 1 day ahead, test years

high_flow_level_and_onset.title: The high-flow level and the onset
high_flow_level_and_onset.words: A basin's high-flow level is the 95th percentile of its daily flow in the training years: a day above it is a high-flow day. A warning is given when the forecast exceeds the level (times a warning level chosen on the validation years). An onset is a high-flow day whose forecast was issued while the river was still at or below the level; 1 day ahead that is exactly the first day of each event (consecutive high-flow days). The 12 basins have 611 onsets in the test years. The share of onsets warned is the main score.
high_flow_level_and_onset.formula: level_b = quantile_0.95(q_mm of basin b over the training years); high day: q > level_b; onset at lead k: q(t+k) > level_b and q(t) <= level_b

verdict.title: The verdict: GO, CAUTION or NOT YET
verdict.words: Criteria fixed before the scores were looked at, applied to the test years at the warning level chosen on the validation years, pooled over the 12 basins and per basin, for all high-flow days and for onsets.

criteria.applied_to: test years, at the warning level chosen on the validation years; separately for all high-flow days and for onsets; pooled over the 12 basins and per basin; lead 1, 2, 3; for lstm_wq, lstm_w and lstm_wqf
criteria.definitions: pod = share of high-flow days that were warned; far = share of warnings that were false; csi = hits / (hits + misses + false alarms)

worked.model: LSTM with the river gauge, 1 day ahead

forecast_rule.title: What a forecast may read
forecast_rule.words: A forecast is issued at the end of day t, knowing the weather (and, for the models with the river gauge, the flow) up to and including day t, and gives the flow of days t+1, t+2 and t+3. A sample belongs to the part of the split that contains its target day. The network is causal (changing later days cannot change an earlier output: asserted before every training).
forecast_rule.formula: forecast(t, k) = f(inputs up to day t), k = 1, 2, 3

gefs_bias_factor_and_issue_time.title: The GEFS forecast: run, local days and bias factor
gefs_bias_factor_and_issue_time.words: The run used is the 00 UTC run of the UTC date t+1 (init_date = t+1): 4 h old at the Eastern issue time in summer, 5 h in winter, 5 or 6 h at the Central one (the latest 00 UTC run that exists at the issue time; the run of the date t+2 starts after it). The days: local day t+k = the wall-clock day of the gauge (zoneinfo America/New_York, America/Chicago for Leaf River, summer time included), forecast hours (lo, hi] of the run with lo = local midnight that starts the day, hi = the one that ends it, counted from the run's start; the amounts of the 3-hourly windows inside the day are summed, a window that straddles a boundary is split in proportion to the time inside (1/3 or 2/3, uniform rain inside a window assumed). The bias factor: bias factor per basin and lead = (sum of the AORC rain of the local days t+k) / (sum of the forecast rain of the same days) over the issue days whose TARGET day t+k lies in the validation years 2000-10-01 .. 2005-09-30 (flood.SPLIT['val']); fc_bc = fc_raw x factor, for every day of 2000-2014 (a factor fitted on the validation years only, applied unchanged to the test years); a single factor per basin and lead: no seasonal correction.
gefs_bias_factor_and_issue_time.formula: factor_(b,k) = sum AORC(t+k) / sum forecast(t+k) over target days in the validation years; forecast_bc = forecast_raw x factor_(b,k)

training_loss_and_stopping.title: Loss and stopping point
training_loss_and_stopping.words: The loss is the squared error of the scaled flow, weighted so that wet and dry basins count nearly alike (the weight is about 1 over the basin's flow variance in the training years). Every 100 updates the model is scored on the validation years of the same basins (mean NSE over basins and leads); the best state is kept and training stops after 6 checks without a gain or at 2,000 updates.
training_loss_and_stopping.formula: loss = mean over scored days of w_b x (forecast_scaled - flow_scaled)^2, w_b = 1 / (sd_b / sd_all + 0.1)^2
